question: Should a 5-person startup use cloud LLM APIs or self-host an open-source model?

plan.main_question: Should a 5-person startup use cloud LLM APIs or self-host an open-source model?
plan.decision_context: A small 5-person startup needs to decide whether to integrate managed cloud LLM APIs or self-host open-source models, balancing limited engineering bandwidth against cost and control.

subquestions.question: What are the comparative monthly costs of cloud LLM APIs versus self-hosting open-source models on cloud GPUs for low to medium request volumes?

decision.rationale: All three specialists are assigned to cover market costs, technical architecture and performance, and risk management respectively, using a standard depth appropriate for this balanced strategic decision.

summaries.sq1: For low to medium request volumes, cloud LLM APIs generally offer a lower total cost than self-hosting. Rented inference-class GPUs cost between $1,100 and $2,900 per month (at $1.50 to $4.00 per hour 24/7) before storage, networking, and engineering labour [ev18]. Because these fixed infrastructure and labour costs are high, self-hosting is more expensive per token at low volumes, with the economic break-even point typically falling between 1 and 3 billion tokens per month [ev19, ev20, ev13].

summaries.sq2: Self-hosting open-source models requires ongoing engineering bandwidth (estimated at 0.25 to 0.5 FTE) to handle driver patches, capacity planning, out-of-memory tuning, and model upgrades [ev6, ev9]. For small teams, this maintenance burden and the risk of unexpected outages (e.g., broken serving containers during updates) can dominate total cost of ownership compared to API integration [ev7, ev8, ev10].
summaries.sq3: Dedicated self-hosted deployments offer faster time-to-first-token latency (median ~120ms vs 250-600ms for shared APIs) and better predictability under normal load, though they require manual scaling or provisioning additional GPUs when concurrency limits are hit [ev14, ev15, ev17]. Shared APIs avoid capacity management but introduce rate limits and higher tail latencies during peak hours [ev15, ev16].

summaries.sq4: Most major hosted AI model providers do not use business API data for training by default [ev1], though prompts and outputs are commonly retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection [ev2]. Enterprise customers may access zero-retention policies via signed data processing agreements [ev3]. While hosted APIs require data to leave internal infrastructure [ev4], self-hosting keeps data within the organization at the cost of shifting full security responsibility to the internal team [ev5].

agreements: Small teams find that engineering labour costs dominate the TCO of self-hosting, making hosted APIs more cost-effective at lower token volumes [ev7, ev12, ev13, ev19, ev20]

report.title: Cloud LLM APIs vs. Self-Hosting for a 5-Person Startup
report.executive_summary: A 5-person startup should use managed cloud LLM APIs rather than self-hosting open-source models. Engineering labor for maintenance and low initial token volumes make self-hosting significantly more expensive and operationally burdensome. This decision depends on maintaining token volumes below the 1 to 3 billion threshold where self-hosting becomes cost-effective.

findings.statement: For organizations with fewer than ten engineers, hosted LLM APIs have a lower total cost of ownership than self-hosting open-weight models when token volume is below several billion per month.
Engineering labor dominates the cost comparison, as self-hosting requires 0.25 to 0.5 of a full-time engineer, outweighing compute savings until token volumes reach several billion per month.

Running a single inference-class GPU 24/7 costs $1,100 to $2,900 per month before storage, networking, and monitoring, making self-hosting more expensive for low volumes below 1 billion tokens where the GPU sits idle.
The break-even point for self-hosting a mid-sized model compared to published API prices falls between 1 and 3 billion tokens per month.
Small teams attempting to self-host face operational risks, including out-of-memory crashes from long prompts, driver update failures, and the need for constant monitoring.

Dedicated deployments offer faster time-to-first-token (around 120 milliseconds) compared to shared APIs (250 to 600 milliseconds), though shared APIs provide flexibility until rate limits or peak-hour latency spikes occur.

Most major hosted API providers do not use business API data for training by default and offer data retention limits of up to 30 days, while zero-retention is available for enterprise customers under a DPA.

limitations: Evidence regarding operational horror stories relies on forum posts which have lower source quality.
Latency and throughput benchmarks come from blog posts rather than rigorous academic studies.
report.recommendation: Use managed cloud LLM APIs now; revisit self-hosting only when token volume consistently exceeds 1 billion tokens per month and dedicated infrastructure engineering headcount can be justified.
